hook.text: What if the OS could take the CPU back in the middle of a burst? That is preemptive scheduling.

srtf.text: S R T F, shortest remaining time first, is the preemptive version of S J F. Now the processes arrive at different times.

srtf1.text: P one starts at zero, with eight to do. At one, P two arrives, needing four.

srtf2.text: P one still has seven left. Four is less. So P two takes the CPU.

srtf3.text: P three and P four arrive, but neither beats what P two has left. Then P four, P one, and P three.

srtf4.text: Average waiting time: six point five.

rr.text: Round robin is first come, first served, plus a timer. Each process runs for at most one time quantum, Q. Then it goes to the back of the queue.

rr1.text: Back to twenty-four, three and three, with a quantum of four. P one runs four, and the timer sends it back.

rr2.text: P two and P three finish inside their turns. Then P one runs alone, all the way to thirty.

rr3.text: Waiting times six, four and seven. Seventeen over three is about five point six seven.

rr4.text: The slide prints five point three. That is an arithmetic slip, so always check your own division.

q.text: The quantum decides everything. Make it huge, and round robin turns into first come, first served.

q2.text: Make it tiny, and the CPU spends its time switching. The quantum must be much larger than a context switch.

pri.text: Priority scheduling gives the CPU to the highest priority. The smallest number is the highest.

pri2.text: Priorities three, one, four, five and two give the order P two, P five, P one, P three, P four. Average wait, eight point two.

starve.text: But a low priority process can wait forever while higher ones keep arriving. That is starvation.

aging.text: The cure is aging. The longer a process waits, the higher its priority grows, until it gets its turn.

ex1.text: S R T F preempts when a shorter job arrives.

ex2.text: Round robin: one quantum, then the back of the queue.

ex4.text: Priority: the smallest number runs first.
